issues.description: The expected signature for addChild per the problem statement and the template is addChild(Person person, Person child) (first parameter = parent, second = child). In the solution, the addChild method has the parameters swapped (public Person addChild(Person child, Person person)), which will compile but causes a semantic mismatch: callers (e.g. PersonResource) pass (person, child) and the solution implementation will treat the parent as the child and vice versa, leading to incorrect behavior and student confusion when comparing template and solution.
issues.suggestedFix: Change the solution's addChild method signature to match the template and problem specification: public Person addChild(Person person, Person child). Update the implementation to validate child.getParents() and add the child to person.getChildren() before saving: if (child.getParents().size() >= 2) throw ...; person.getChildren().add(child); return personRepository.save(person);

issues.description: The problem statement and the template define the service method addChild with signature addChild(Person person, Person child) (parent first, child second). In the solution, the method's parameter order and names are swapped (addChild(Person child, Person person)), reversing the semantic roles of the two parameters. This creates a mapping confusion: callers (e.g., PersonResource) pass (person, child) expecting the first argument to be the parent, but the solution implementation treats the first parameter as the child. Students reading the problem statement and template would reasonably implement and call addChild(parent, child); the solution's differing parameter order is an unintended inconsistency that increases cognitive load and may lead to incorrect behavior or confusion.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the solution's addChild signature and parameter semantics match the problem statement and template: change the solution method to public Person addChild(Person person, Person child) and ensure the implementation treats the first parameter as the parent (e.g., person.getChildren().add(child); return personRepository.save(person);). Alternatively, update all callers (PersonResource and tests) and the problem text to consistently use the swapped parameter order, but aligning the solution to the original (person, child) is the least surprising fix.
